Title: A seeded user with the correct password gets a token that authorizes GET /orders
Technique(s): Equivalence partitioning, partition "known username + correct password"
Preconditions: - alice is seeded and has no failed login in the last 60 s
Test Data:
- username: alice — the "known username" partition
- password: the shared example password — the "correct password" partition
Steps:
1. Post alice's username and correct password to POST /auth/login.
2. Call GET /orders with the returned token.
Expected Results:
1. The login answers 200 and the body carries a non-empty `token`.
Evidence: “A seeded user who posts the correct password to POST /auth/login receives 200 and a token” — AC-AUTH-001
2. GET /orders with that token answers 200 with a JSON array (the token is accepted).
Evidence: “a token that authorizes GET /orders for the next 60 minutes” — AC-AUTH-001
Notes:
Level: api
Smoke: yes
Source: cases/auth-login-lockout.md

Title: An unknown username gets the same status and body as a wrong password

Evidence: “nothing in status, body, headers or timing distinguishes them” — BR-AUTH-001

Title: The fifth failed login answers 401 and the sixth answers 429 with Retry-After: 60
Technique(s): Boundary value analysis on the failed-attempt count, values 4 / 5 / 6 around the limit 5; state transition open -> locked
Preconditions: - probe-<run id> has no failed login in the last 60 s (true by construction: the name is new)
Test Data:
- username: probe-<run id> — failures count per submitted username, known or not (BR-AUTH-001 Audit line)
- attempt 4 — just below the limit; attempt 5 — on the limit; attempt 6 — just above it
Steps: 1. Post a wrong password for probe-<run id> six times within 60 s, keeping each answer.
Expected Results:
1. Attempts 1 to 5 each answer 401 with the body {"error": "invalid credentials"}; attempt 4 and attempt 5 are checked explicitly.
Evidence: “The fifth failed login for one username within 60 seconds answers 401” — AC-AUTH-004
2. Attempt 6 answers 429 with the header Retry-After: 60 and the body exactly {"error": "too many attempts"}.
Evidence: “the sixth answers 429 with the header Retry-After: 60 and the body {"error": "too many attempts"}.” — AC-AUTH-004
Notes:
Level: api  (the username is unique per run, so the lockout touches no shared user and the case runs in parallel)
Source: cases/auth-login-lockout.md

Title: Every forbidden transition answers 409 invalid transition and leaves the order unchanged

Preconditions: - per row, an order of alice in the row's status (shipped and cancelled reached through the lifecycle actions)
Test Data:
- row 1: paid, pay, alice — repeated pay
- row 2: new, ship, carol — not paid yet
- row 3: shipped, pay, alice — terminal
- row 4: shipped, ship, carol — terminal, repeated ship
- row 5: shipped, cancel, alice — terminal
- row 6: cancelled, pay, alice — terminal
- row 7: cancelled, ship, carol — terminal
- row 8: cancelled, cancel, carol — terminal, repeated cancel
Steps:
1. As the row's actor, POST /orders/{id}/<action>.
2. As alice, GET /orders/{id}.
Expected Results:
1. Step 1 answers 409 with the body exactly {"error": "invalid transition"}.
Evidence: “pay on a paid order, ship on a new order, and any action on a shipped or cancelled order each answer 409 with the body {"error": "invalid transition"}” — AC-ORD-033
2. Step 2 shows the status the order had before step 1, and `paid_at` unchanged (null for row 2).
Evidence: “and the status is unchanged.” — AC-ORD-033

Title: The note-length outcome is the same for every caller, status and character set
Technique(s): Pairwise (13 rows, verified by pairwise.py; design-tables.md#pairwise-note-validation) + syntax testing on multi-byte characters
Preconditions:
- per row: for "edit", an order of alice in the row's status with note "first"; for "create", no order
- alice owns fewer than 4 orders in status new
Test Data:
- ascii text: "a" repeated to the row's length
- vietnamese text: "ệ" (U+1EC7, precomposed, 3 bytes in UTF-8) repeated to the row's length; 200 of them are 600 bytes
- length 0 on edit is {"note": ""}; length 0 on create is an empty body
Steps:
1. As the row's caller, send the row's operation (POST /orders, or PATCH /orders/{id}) with the row's note.
2. As alice, GET /orders/{id} (edit rows) or GET /orders (create rows).
Expected Results:
1. Rows with length 0 or 200 answer 201 (create) or 200 (edit), and the returned and re-read note equal the sent string character for character, so 200 vietnamese characters (600 bytes) are accepted.
Evidence: “`note` is a string of 0 to 200 characters (characters, not bytes).” — BR-ORD-003
2. Rows with length 201 answer 400 with an error naming `note`; an edited order still shows "first" and a create adds no order.
Evidence: “PATCH /orders/{id} with a note of 201 characters answers 400 and the note is unchanged.” — AC-ORD-024
Assumptions: rows with caller manager-same-tenant assume OQ-006 option A (a manager may create and edit notes); rows with status paid, shipped or cancelled assume OQ-005 option A (the note is editable in every status); rows with length 201 assume OQ-002 option A (rejected). Rows 1 and 12 depend on no question.

Title: The sixth open order is refused with 409 and the customer still owns exactly 5 new orders
Technique(s): Boundary value analysis on the open-order count, 4 -> 5 (on the cap) and 5 -> 6 (just above)
Preconditions:
- alice owns exactly 4 orders in status new (setup creates or cancels orders of alice to reach 4)
- order.open_cap has its default value 5
Test Data: - count before step 1: 4 — just below the cap; count before step 2: 5 — on the cap
Steps:
1. As alice, POST /orders with {"note": "fifth"}.
2. As alice, POST /orders with {"note": "sixth"}.
3. As alice, GET /orders and count the orders in status new.
Expected Results:
1. Step 1 answers 201 with `status` "new" (the fifth open order is allowed).
Evidence: “A customer may have at most 5 orders in status” — BR-ORD-007
2. Step 2 answers 409 with the body exactly {"error": "too many open orders"} and no `id`.
Evidence: “A customer who already owns 5 orders in status "new" answers 409 with the body {"error": "too many open orders"} on the next POST /orders” — AC-ORD-006
3. Step 3 counts exactly 5 orders in status new, and no order has the note "sixth".
Evidence: “and still owns exactly 5 new orders.” — AC-ORD-006
Assumptions: the cap of 5 orders in new and the 409 refusal (results 1 to 3) are option B of OQ-003; nothing in S1 limits open orders
Notes:
Level: api
Exclusive: yes — asserts alice's exact count of orders in new
Source: cases/order-open-cap.md
